title: Slope limits reduced British butterfly growth forecast error but gave no clear gain over a recent mean in 2015-2024
abstract: Can changes to a climate-model slope repair later forecast failure? We tested sequential updates on published annual statistics for 106 Swiss plant phases and British butterfly species. Models fit through 2004. Updates used only ten past annual pairs before each 2015-2024 prediction. A slope limited to zero through one improved butterfly growth skill by 0.171 over a level-only update (nominal 95% interval 0.046 to 0.309). But its skill against a recent response mean was only 0.015 (-0.069 to 0.098). Only 15 of 36 growth species improved over the level-only update. A free slope added error, and adaptive weights gave no clear gain over a fixed half-weight blend. For spring plants, a level update kept skill of 0.645; limiting the slope gave 0.624. An overlapping older-model panel gave the same growth repair without clear added skill over a recent mean. An exact error identity separated alignment with old error from the cost of changing forecasts. The study tests old observations with observed target-year weather, not issued weather forecasts. Short annual records, joint density-weather growth increments and changing site coverage limit inference. Code, aggregate performance results, source hashes, figures and independent arithmetic checks are included.
